# Copper January 2011 

- Copper kicked off the year with a bit of a hangover, declining on a bout of profit taking, in addition to concerns over Eurozone debt levels and Chinese measures to cool economic activity.  Supply side news then renewed the focus on the expected market deficit this year and although this sparked considerable interest in seeing five-figure prices the heat fell away as all market chatter suddenly switched to rising exchange stock levels as well as the probable decline in Chinese orders as the new Lunar Year approached. However, we are sure the $10,000/t level will be hit sooner rather than later and have upped our estimate for Q1 average prices to $9,300/t. 

- The current demand picture is somewhat blurred, with strong momentum from last year carrying through into January for Europe but activity in China at a pre New Year lull.  Indeed, the pick-up in industrial activity in the final quarter of 2010 has helped to propel bookings into January in Europe, with some rod buyers even pointing to scarcity of material.  Moreover, as concern over the debt crisis eases, credit availability is also improving.  Curiously, the reverse is true in China, which is in the midst of a seasonal slowdown in demand ahead of the New Year, while credit is becoming increasingly hard to come by.  However, a post-festivities upturn in production at semis fabricators will not necessarily feed through immediately into increased apparent refined demand given the level of stocks both on and off exchange in China. 

- In previous years the catalyst for many settlements in the annual copper concentrate Mating Season has been the establishment of a single deal between a major buyer and seller that has been viewed by the market as the “benchmark”.  However, for 2011, a new settlement dynamic has entered the market with buyers apparently being offered terms that reference the spot market in order to establish TC/RCs with a view to setting several sets of terms on this basis over the contractual period.  Time will tell whether this new approach will become more widely accepted across the market.  That said given that a number of long-term contracts covering a large tonnage of concentrates have already been finalised at $56/t &5.6c/lb buyers and sellers looking for standard reference terms to facilitate concluding their contracts are likely to opt for these numbers as the benchmark for the 2011 Mating Season.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**Copper ends 2010 with a bang** LME copper prices held their very own New Year’s party slightly ahead of the due date, with cash running up by US$350/t in the final three trading days of the year to end at a record high US$9739/t ($4.42/lb) on the 31<sup>st</sup> , or US$1200/t up within the month.  Equally, the backwardation edged further out to 3.5c/lb by the end of the month, almost double what it was on December 1<sup>st</sup> .  The party mode continued on the first day back at the office, but then a correction ensued as profit-taking kicked in on January 5<sup>th</sup> , knocking prices back down to US$9461/t ($4.29/lb – cash).  But it was a different story the following week, as concern about Eurozone debt levels and Chinese government actions over dousing the economy kept the trading range in copper to a minor US$240/t.  However, the lead-up to the 19<sup>th</sup> – the third trading Wednesday of the month – brought renewed upside pressure on prices, and that day saw another record level set at US$9788/t ($4.44/lb).  But although this sparked considerable interest in seeing five-figure prices – which we are sure will come sooner rather than later – the heat fell away as all market chatter suddenly focused on the rising stock levels of physical metal on all exchanges as well as the probable decline in Chinese orders as the new Lunar Year approached.  By the 25<sup>th</sup> , cash dipped to what will probably be the month’s low of US$9330/t ($4.23/lb), and the backwardation had once again narrowed to just 0.6c/lb. 

**Collahuasi’s strike – then the port accident – buoyed prices through to January** If one of the reasons why copper strengthened during December was the strike at the 550kt/a Collahuasi mine in Chile, then the successful conclusion to negotiations as early as the 7<sup>th</sup> of that month should have capped the price surge.  But prices retained their momentum for the following week.  Copper bulls then placed their faith on the fact that the subsequent accident on the 18<sup>th</sup> at the Punta Patache export terminal that Collahuasi uses would support prices.  Indeed, this did prompt a declaration of force majeure on concentrates shipments from what is the world’s third largest mine, and so the bulls’ intent regarding prices became self-fulfilling all the way through to the New Year.  By then, the mine’s owners (Anglo American/Xstrata Copper et al) re-routed around 70% of the feed through to Antofagasta, and this contributed to the fall in prices on the 4<sup>th</sup> . Additional material has also been shipped out of Arica port since the 19<sup>th</sup> . 

**But despite the mid-month price fall, it does not take much to prompt nerv

ousness in this market** Even though it is a significant mine in terms of supply, the Collahuasi port issue was a tenuous hold on price support at these elevated levels. Once it became known that even reduced shipment levels were getting out, there was very little else in the market place to keep copper prices on the boil. The initial take on lower Chinese copper imports in December (down by 2% on November levels), plus mounting concerns over Portugal’s likely need for a bail-out, conspired to suppress prices across the LME complex through to the 11th . By then, though, the European Central Bank helped Portugal out by buying up a bond issue, and the release of a handful of positive economic data from the USA and China helped to shrug off any lingering depression. Cash edged up US$100/t on the 11th alone, and then by a further $140/t on the 12th, aided in part by news from Chile of a fire at Codelco’s Andina underground mine. Both events in Latin America gave off more smoke than fire, ultimately, as Andina’s miners were able to return to work within hours, and Cerro Verde remained open after a compromise was reached on the 14th itself. However, it does show that in these times of relatively balanced markets (but slipping into an acknowledged considerable deficit for this year), it does not take very much to punt metal prices up at all. The small price sell-off on that Friday 14th was also pushed partly by a story that Chinese copper supply was more than satisfactory, given the holidays that lay ahead. In some ways, this Metals Market Service Monthly Update - January 2011 Page 2 of 21 Copper Monthly Update is true, but the reality is always much more complex than a single story would suggest, and by the following Monday 17th the market re-focused on what is likely to be a global metal shortage this year, and all concern over a three-week halt to Chinese buying fell away – temporarily. **Prices likely to stay in a narrow range until beyond the Chinese holidays** Since then, though, the market has been stuck in a relatively narrow range of US$450/t as players try to gauge which way to go. The bullish view rests on an outlook spanning the month after February 8th when the Chinese return from their holidays. Meanwhile, the bears point to the rising exchange stock levels, declining spot market premia across some regional markets, and select black spots in the global economy. As expected, there are elements of the truth to both. **Stocks rise on the LME and Comex…** Rising stock levels on two of the three physical exchanges are clearly visible. On the LME, stocks rose by 25kt during December to 377kt, and now stand within a hair of touching the 400kt mark that was last seen in August, having risen on all but three days this month. On a smaller scale, Comex stocks have also risen, from just under 59kt at the start of the month, to >62kt by the 27th . Meanwhile, in Shanghai, stocks have held firm at 130-132kt during the month, and there is little rationale to see this falling this side of the Chinese holidays. **..but the strengthening backwardation has been a contributing factor** Although higher stocks appear to reflect nothing more than the disparity between supply and demand, material will also be drawn onto exchanges under the favourable economics of a periodic backwardation. LME copper has been in a back since November 9th . At that time, stocks on the LME stood at 364kt, and mostly continued to decline to 349kt over the following four weeks. But as the backwardation became more consistent and entrenched, stocks have increased by almost 50kt since December 9th . **Spot premia levels also somewhat misleading in our view** Equally, we have witnessed falling spot premia in some important markets, yet firming elsewhere. The US and Chinese markets have been showing softening premia this month, for example, with metal in the USA attracting a premium of between 5.0-5.5c/lb of late (down from 5.75c/lb), and a Chinese refined metal import premium of only between US$30-60/t. From the two, the Chinese figure would appear a more accurate reflection of the markets there, given the widely acknowledged metal surplus and the low levels of manufacturing activity that have been in place for over the past month. The latter will continue right through to the end of the Chinese holidays on February 8th. In addition, we hear that there are large tonnages of refined copper in Chinese bonded warehouses (some estimates suggest the figure is 500kt) ready to fulfill that market’s requirements when demand picks up. In the US, though, there is the belief that when fabricators were caught short of metal during early 2009, they entered into a higher proportion than normal of contract

business. Consequently, spot premia are suffering because there is less need to be active in the spot market for metal. **Europe, on the other hand, is witnessing firming premia** The US$90-100/t level for Grade A and Chilean material that we have seen over the last three months or so applies more so to the Rotterdam market; for shipments to northern Germany, we are told this edges up to US$115/t. Clearly, Codelco’s own European premia level of US$98/t is setting a new standard, but we also learn that there has been almost no deviation from this price at all; in past years, some level of discount or ease of financing would be granted, but this has not been the case so far. This also dovetails into the comments we are hearing that cathode supplies into Europe are somewhat tighter, especially given that Russian cathode is slow in coming through due to the imposition of the new tax on cathode exports. Norilsk Nickel, for example, has shown little interest in sending cathode into Europe since the imposition of the tax. **Economic malaise in consumer regions ebbing - mostly** We also consider that the third “leg” of the bearish argument for lower prices during this first quarter – global economic malaise – is losing credibility. In the US, at least, consumer confidence is notably picking up and indeed, there is more belief now that people will get a job even if they do not currently have one. Companies are making investment decisions, even if this has largely been directed to capital rather than labour to date. In our mining sector at least, companies are re-opening mines shuttered during the last recession, and ordering trucks and tyres at a sufficient rate that there is once again some concern about backlogs extending out and costs going up. Meanwhile, with China missing its new loans targets again in December, the concern that the government will continue to impose more restrictive measures lives on in to 2011; equally, no matter what the European Central Bank says or does, the issue of excessive debt continues to rear its ugly head across several countries and remains a justifiable concern for the metal bears. **Price forecasts and world quarterly supply/demand balance – (kt)** |||**Refined**

The most responsive has already been seen in all markets of higher scrap availability and use, and at attractive prices. In Europe, mulberry grades (No. 1 scrap) are running at a discount to the lowest LME cathode grade of c.US$100/t, for example, while in China, lower scrap grades (No. 2) cost up to US$1000-1500/t less than imported refined metal. Scrap imported into China last year rose by over 9% to a record 4.2Mt. If cathode supplies remain tight during the course of this year, as we expect, and Chinese copper demand grows by our forecast 7% y-o-y, refined copper imports will remain at the current 200-230kt/month level, and the demand growth gap will have to be met by higher scrap use. The downside here for Chinese scrap processors, users and traders is that the government has now eliminated the 50% VAT rebate on scrap use which will make the material more costly, whether it is generated domestically or imported. However, to put this into context, the rebate is essentially a subsidy and this is being withdrawn, while the price discount still makes it well worth semis producers while to use scrap. Given the reluctance of end users to pay current high prices, this suggests lower margins at semis fabricators in addition to at least some widening of scrap spreads but not a dramatic shift away from scrap consumption towards refined material. In fact, we expect total copper consumption running ahead of refined demand, owing to expected tightness in the refined market. Our overall market balances for 2011 and 2012 are little changed from last month’s report and hence our price forecasts remain unchanged also. We expect cash quotes to average $9,700/t ($4.13/lb) this year and $7,900/t ($3.58/lb) next year. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - January 2011 Page 5 of 21

## Consumption 

The current demand picture is somewhat blurred, with strong momentum from last year carrying through into January for Europe but activity in China at a pre New Year lull.  Indeed, the pick up in industrial activity in the final quarter of 2010 has helped to propel bookings into January in Europe, with some rod buyers even pointing to scarcity of material. Moreover, as concern over the debt crisis eases, credit availability is also improving.  Curiously, the reverse is true in China, which is in the midst of a seasonal slowdown in demand ahead of the New Year, while credit is becoming increasingly hard to come by.  However, a post festivities upturn in production at semis fabricators will not necessarily feed through immediately into increased apparent refined demand given the level of stocks both on and off exchange in China. 

### **Europe and CIS** 

**IP growth picks up in final months of last year** Having been stagnant through Q3, IP growth picked up in Q4.  Euro zone output expanded by 1.2% in November m-o-m and by 7.3% y-o-y, while EU 27 growth was 1.4% and 7.8%, respectively.  For the first 11 months in total, Euro zone IP expanded by 7% y-o-y.  The main area strength was in capital goods, while consumer durables were pretty weak, suggesting that Euro businesses have been more inclined to invest in capital than labour. 

European lead indicators improved in December, as the headline PMI went from 55.7 to 57.3.  The new orders PMI reached 58.2, signalling the fastest expansion since Q2 2010.  Individual country data suggest that Germany and the core nations will continue to grow the strongest, but there were also encouraging signs that manufacturing is starting to improve in peripherals such as Spain and Ireland, and this should translate into improved output in Q1 this year. 

**Debt issues less of a concern** The main cloud hanging over Europe last year was the debt crisis.  Although fundamentally little has changed over the past month or so, there have been developments that have resulted in more optimism.  China and Japan have declared support for the euro and appear willing to buy government debt.  There are also rumours that European politicians are formulating extensive coordinated action in the near term that will be designed to quell further concern over other economies such as Spain and Portugal.  As a result, the euro has rallied against the dollar in recent weeks. 

**Strong demand for copper remains in place in Europe** In spite of these financial concerns, though, European copper demand was strong for much of 2010, and this momentum appears to have continued into early 2011.  We are hearing that stocks of wire rod and even of some wire products are virtually nil, and that customers are not only prepared to pay for material when it is available, but also have access to the finance to do so.  This suggests that the prior difficulty that several companies have faced in obtaining credit

or bridging loans might well be coming to an end.  It is too early to say, though, if these optimistic conditions will persist throughout the quarter, and so we have kept our European demand figures largely in place since our last report.  But it is somewhat encouraging, and should such commentary prevail into February, then it is likely that we will edge our demand figures up for the region from the flat outlook that we have this year vs. 2010. 

What is preventing us from doing so now is that much of the strength in eurozone copper demand has stemmed from the robust automotive sector in Germany and elsewhere.  But VAT rises in 5 countries and fiscal cutbacks are likely to impact on demand in H1 in particular, leaving the regional auto outlook for 2011 anything but clear.  Equally, in the construction sector, both commercial and civil activity is likely to contract through 2011, offsetting any possible gains in the residential sector where the UK and Germany offer the best prospects of mild recovery. 

**Russian rod not evident yet** Although the new export tax on Russian cathode kicked in mid-December, rod buyers in Europe say that there has not yet been any sudden rush of Russian rod availability in their markets.  Total Russian rod exports reached only 128kt in the Jan-Oct period last year, _vs._ 210kt for all of 2009.  Adding to the general tightness in Europe of both spot cathode and rod has been the disappearance from the market of rod from Slovakia.  Despite the general strength of the European copper sector,  Kovohuty a.s., located at Krompachy in eastern Slovakia, is unlikely to benefit by it, for it is reportedly offline and may not return to production until March at the earliest.  However, it is not clear if the stoppage is for a technical reason, or if it is related to the financial restructuring being carried out by its ultimate parent company, A-TEC Industries of Austria, which began during the final quarter of last year.  A-TEC’s need for financial restructuring has just resulted in the successful sale of its machine tool manufacturing subsidiary, Dцrries Scharmann, this month to a Swiss group for €70M. 

Kovohuty has been a small producer (5-44kt/a) of copper anode from scrap over the last ten years, and was able to restart its copper rod plant in 2006 (200t) when Montanwerke Brixlegg of Austria (another A-TEC subsidiary) took ownership.  Most of the anode from Kovohuty (44kt in 2010 from a capacity raised to 60kt/a in 2008, after a 646M Sk investment) is sent to Brixlegg for processing into cathode (which produced 96.2kt in 2009) and copper shapes (83kt), while rod output at Kovohuty itself has also increased year on year to 30.3kt in 2008 and c.36kt in 2009 – the most recent figure available.  Besides Brixlegg and Kovohuty, A-TEC’s other copper-related division is the bar and wire products distribution company, Gindre Duchavany S.A., which originated in France but has since expanded its coverage to the UK, Germany and Spain i

n Europe, plus the USA, Russia and India.

### **Americas** 

**US economy gains belief** There are signs that US recovery is becoming self-reinforcing, as stronger business sales feed through into increased hiring and further capital investment.  This should help to reduce unemployment through the year – which is the most important concern for Main Street now – and leaving the outlook much improved from only a few months ago. 

**PMI jumps in December** Leading indicators suggest that US manufacturing could be gaining momentum once again. The new orders component of the PMI jumped from 56.9 to 60.9 in December, well above the expansion threshold of 50. Wood Mackenzie recently upgraded its 2011 forecast for IP growth in the US from 1.9% to 3%, reflecting the increased optimism and prospects following the announcement of further fiscal stimulus. 

**Both industrial output and plant utilisation improve during 2010** However, we are still in the phase where data comparisons can always clash, depending on the periods used.  US industrial output growth accelerated in December, to end the year on a higher note, after months of poor growth.  December growth was boosted by high utilities output due to the extremely cold weather.  But total Q4 output expanded by just 0.6% q-o-q, and growth for 2010 as a whole was 5.7%, leaving output around 2004 levels.  At the end of the year, capacity utilisation reached 76%, the highest level since August 2008, but still almost 5% below average utilisation between 1972 and 2009. 

**US auto sector has strong 2010 vs. 2009, but still at low levels** US auto production had a fairly weak end to 2010, with December growth of just 3.1% y-o-y.  For 2010 as a whole, though, output expanded by 35.9% to 7.7m units.  While this is a big improvement on 2009, it was still the second lowest annual total we have on record going back to 1978. However, anecdotal information suggests the US auto market has made a solid start to the year, with sales in the first half of January running up by around 18% y-o-y.  With an improved us economic outlook, our forecast for 7.4% production growth in 2011 would appear to be conservative. 

**Construction sector shows little life** US residential construction ended the year on a low note, as housing starts in December fell 4.3% to an annualised 529k units, the lowest level in over a year.  Single family units were hit the hardest. For 2010 as a whole starts rose by 5.8%, the first year of growth since 2006.  Permits surged, but this largely due to builders trying to gain approval before legislation changes.  With sales remaining very low and a huge stock of properties, there is still little reason to add more supply of new homes. 

**Copper rod production, shipments up by c.10% to November** Continuing the difficulty in making “fair” comparisons, data from the American Bureau of Metal Statistics (ABMS) s

how that apparent domestic consumption of wire rod fell in November 2010 by 5.1% from the prior month, to 93kt, but increased by 12% on the same month in 2009. For the 11month period last year, apparent rod consumption was up by 6.4% to 1.12Mt (metric). Meanwhile, domestic shipments of rod were up by 10.2% to 1.155Mt; with production up by a slightly lower 9.8% to 1.17Mt, rod stocks declined from 21.6kt at the end of November 2009, to 15.4kt a year later. #### **US copper wire rod production – (kt)** 40 125

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - January 2011 Page 7 of 21 Copper Monthly Update ### **China** **Economic data turns up the heat on central bankers** Industrial production growth accelerated once again in December to 13.5% year on year, resulting in 2010 growth of 15.7%, while GDP growth also advanced in Q4, from 9.6% to 9.8%. The strong end to the year in IP growth owed much large gains in transportation, machinery and equipment. However, the rapid pace of growth in spite of recent policy tightening sparked fears of overheating and further rate rises, despite the mild easing in CPI in December. Significant increases in reserve requirements and possibly interest rates are expected in next 6 months. China picked up the pace of renminbi appreciation at the end of year, with its real effective exchange rate gaining 1.7% in December and 4.7% for the year as a whole. With inflation in China running well above that of the USA, the pace of appreciation is actually much greater than it seems. With this situation likely to continue, the 3% nominal appreciation we expect in 2011 would be more like 7% in real terms, hastening China’s shift away from exports. Chinese fixed asset investment increased by 23.8% in 2010, or by 19.5% in real terms. The total number was slightly below expectations, and the December split shows a sharp slowdown in year on year growth to 16%, from 29% in November. Looking at the breakdown of the data for 2010, the strongest growth came from real-estate, non ferrous metals and local governments. An NDRC researcher has estimated that FIA growth will likely slow to ~20% this year, as credit tightening continues. This would be well below the 26% average of the past 7 years. **Floor to fall from under construction market?** Chinese construction data for December pointed to some possible alarming developments. Floor space under construction for 2010 totalled 27%, down from 29% in Jan-Nov. This basically suggests that year on year growth in floor space under construction fell below 5% in December. This cannot be explained by a rush of completions at the end of the year, as comple

tions slowed even more sharply. For 2010, floor space completed grew by 5% but had been running at 10+% growth through the first 11 months. Floor space started, on the other hand, grew by 42% y-o-y in 2010. The data as a whole reinforces the idea that we have discussed previously, that China potentially has a very large amount of property sitting near completion that is being held back from the market to avoid depressing prices. This clearly has direct implications for demand for the building wire segment as stocks of unsold properties will become an increasing drag on working capital, especially given tightening credit conditions. **Consumers to apply the brakes on car purchases** Chinese auto production accelerated once again in December to a record high, according to provisional data. Output expanded by 23.9% y-o-y in December, taking total 2010 to 18.6 million units – 32% y-o-y growth. Figures toward year end were aided by a rush of purchases before tax incentives expired in the new year. In order to cool the fast-growing auto market, the Ministry of Finance announced that, from Jan 1st , the central government would end its two-year tax incentives for small cars and subsidies to farmers. In addition, Beijing, one of the largest car markets in China, started to restrict car license applications from end of December. Clearly, this points to a more sedentary pace of demand from the auto sector in the near term. #### **Chinese production of copper semis – (kt)** 80 1100

**Demand strips off another layer…** Sheet/strip demand continued to weaken in January, with some strip makers complaining of difficulty passing on high copper prices to their customers. **New settlement dynamic introduced into Mating Season negotiations** In previous years the catalyst for many settlements in the annual copper concentrate Mating Season has been the establishment of a single deal between a major buyer and seller that has been viewed by the market as the “benchmark”.  The 2009 benchmark of $75/t & 7.5c/lb was set by Freeport and MMC just prior to Christmas 2008 while for 2010, Freeport and SMM established the $46.5/t & 4.65c/lb reference terms during the third week of December 2009.  However, for 2011, a new settlement dynamic has entered the market with buyers apparently being offered two options by BHP Billiton, acting on behalf of Escondida.  The first option relates to the conventional fixing of one set of TC/RCs to cover the following 12 month brick or block period. The second option references the spot market in order to establish TC/RCs with a view to setting several sets of terms on this basis over the contractual period.  This shift in BHP Billiton’s marketing strategy towards spot market referencing stems from an apparent corporate desire to be viewed as a price taker and not a price setter.  This would also bring the company’s copper concentrates marketing objectives into line with its existing coal and iron ore pricing policies. 

**Spot market referencing in long-term market – not without its complexities** Superficially, the linking of long-term deals to spot prices should take away a lot of the angst involved in having to undertake a number of rounds of negotiations once or twice per year to eventually fix terms on the basis of each party’s view of the outlook for the copper concentrates market.  Also, given the large number of deals that are transacted on an ongoing basis in the spot market, referencing long-term TC/RCs in this manner should, at least in theory, lead to a more representative or fairer pricing structure for each party involved.  However, the spot market is fraught with complexities that could, potentially, open up a minefield of problems for buyers and sellers alike.  For example, the two distinct sets of spot market TC/RCs that run concurrently can be materially different depending upon timing issues and price spreads.  Quite often the spot terms paid by traders to miners are significantly higher or lower than those that the same traders receive from smelters on account of QP differentials and

also depending upon when the buy and sell trades are transacted (some traders will take large open positions on the basis of their perceptions of the market outlook as a means of generating far larger profits than could be achieved through a more straightforward similarly-timed buy/sell approach.  Apart from QPs, traders are also able to profit from differences in other side terms (i.e. payment terms, gold and silver payables and RCs, penalty charges etc.).  Independent observers, such as ourselves that report spot terms, often only have the benefit of the headline TC/RCs and not the full suite of side term adjustments that can distort the true value of each spot deal.  This means that these series of spot rates are indicative only and, therefore, cannot be relied upon as some form of benchmark for this market.  In addition, transactions in the spot market are notoriously “lumpy” with many months often passing with little or no business having been carried out.  Whether or not buyers and sellers would be prepared to fix new long-term TC/RCs on indicative spot rates is not, as yet, clear.  One final observation on this subject relates to China’s growing dominance in the spot market and its potential ability to influence terms.  Between August and October 2010 spot rates soared from $15/t & 1.5c/lb to $78/t & 7.8c/lb as a direct result of Chinese buyers withdrawing from the market.  Whether this was more by chance or through a concerted effort is an interesting point but the obvious question has to be, if Chinese buyers have achieved this result once already, what is to stop them replicating this (at least in part) ahead of each spot-related long-term negotiation?

**First Quantum targets aggressive expansion plans** Following rece

nt setbacks in the DRC involving ownership disputes at the Kolwezi Tailings project and the Frontier mine, Canada’s First Quantum Minerals has recently announced an aggressive expansion program at a number of its mines and projects south of the DRC border.  The company recorded a 13.7% decline in copper production to 322.7kt in 2010 mainly on account of the premature closure of Frontier. However, at Kansanshi, an expansion is underway to raise annual copper output from 250kt/a to 400kt/a in 2015.  This is to be implemented in two phases.  Phase 1 will cost $40M and will see an increase in production to ~285kt/a from Q4 2011.  It is focused on raising the capacity of the oxide circuit by about 20% to 8.5Mt/a and building in flexibility to allow for the mixed and sulphide circuits to be switched as needed to suit mining activity. The expansion will include the use of relocated equipment from the recently closed Bwana Mkubwa copper Sx/Ew plant.  Construction of Phase 2 is expected to start in the second half of 2012 with commissioning targeted for the first half of 2014. This phase of the expansion will focus on the construction of a new concentrator with a planned annual throughput of 25Mt/a bringing the mine’s overall output to 400kt/a at a cost of $350M.  First Quantum is also hopeful that its Sentinel project, also in Zambia, will shape up to be of a similar scale to Kansanshi with a potential output range of 250kt/a to 370kt/a.  An NI-43-101 compliant resource is not expected until mid-2011 but the company is aiming for initial design and construction phases to commence in 2011 with production as early as 2014.  Given the very substantial potential increase in copper-inconcentrate production from its Zambian mines and projects First Quantum is also examining the economics of constructing and operating a greenfield copper smelter (300kt/a?) in the country.  The company is also developing its Kevitsa nickel-copper project in Finland which is expected to produce 15-20kt/a of copper-in-concentrates while the Haquira project in Peru that it acquired through its takeover of Antares Minerals, could be capable of producing 230kt/a Cu from sulphide and oxide reserves.  First Quantum believes that it can increase copper output to 470kt/a by 2015 based on existing development commitments and by a further 500kt/a if the Sentinel and Haquira projects are brought on stream as currently envisaged.
